latest.title: UK says EU reset deal agreed but talks will continue ‘in some areas’ – live
latest.summary: UK statement comes after EU said deal would not take effect without future agreement over university tuition fees Senior correspondent Making today’s reset deal contingent on a further agreement on the level of tuition fees for EU citizens is designed to neutralise the leverage London gets in the next six months, EU sources have said. Senior diplomats had already confirmed this week that the EU would defer the deal on the level of tuition fees for another six months , a move designed to give the UK leverage in parallel negotiations to have the UK included in Made in Europe legislation designed to protect EU supply chains against China. But the move to make the food and drink deal also contingent on a tuition fees deal effectively seeks to neutralise the leverage the UK gets today. This is a serious chess game and shows the EU, again, is willing to speak very warmly about the UK but will play absolute hard ball when it comes to conceding any points to a former member state. It was the same point France was making last night insisting the UK could not have voting rights on legislation in relation to food and drink. During his meeting with businesses in Brussels, PM Burnham said his EU deal would add up to 0.5% to the UK’s GDP. “We’re pretty much there, and it’s a really good deal.” “Treasury analysis out today is saying that now it’s clear up to 0.5% on GDP as a result of the deal. The single biggest growth intervention in this Parliament.” Continue reading...

Sports.title: Lewis Hamilton is now the apex sports protester as US athletes stay silent
Sports.summary: The Ferrari driver has always used his fame to highlight causes he cares about. Now he stands out as other athletes tone down their rhetoric Most Formula One drivers might slip away to the beach or the golf course on a week off between races. Lewis Hamilton is not most drivers, though. Instead he went to the Rafah border crossing between Egypt and Gaza. He greeted aid workers in Arabic, toured the checkpoint and visited the Egyptian Red Crescent warehouses in nearby El-Arish, where relief supplies are prepared for distribution. Hamilton made the visit on a day Israeli airstrikes and gunfire killed at least seven Palestinians in Gaza, adding to a death toll that’s climbed above 74,000 since war broke out three years ago. He wore dark glasses and dressed head to toe in black. “The past three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling,” he wrote on Instagram of his visit, before turning the lens on himself. “I know so many people that feel that same helplessness. That same need to do something rather than watch. I don’t want us to get used to their suffering. I don’t want us to look away.” Continue reading...

Culture.title: The Match review – Lineker, Shilton et al look back at England’s ‘hand of God’ clash with Argentina
Culture.summary: Argentinian co-directors Juan Cabral and Santiago Franco work hard to appear impartial in account that situates the game in a long continuum of conflict Here is a football documentary that is a cut above the drain-clogging content that loiters in streaming platforms everywhere. Its subject is the World Cup quarter-final contest between Argentina and England in 1986, a game constantly replayed in the collective consciousness for the two never-to-be-forgotten moments contributed by Diego Maradona: the illicit “hand of God” goal that gave Argentina the lead, and then five minutes later his sublime second goal, for which he skipped past half a dozen of the England team before slotting the ball home with the outside of his foot. It was this second strike, voted in 2002 as Fifa’s goal of the century , that partly lanced the boil of English rage over Maradona’s outrageous cheating; what could they do in the face of such authentic genius? Over and above football matters, it’s clear to see that there were bigger things at stake. Rather obviously, it happened only four years after the Falklands war, which thoroughly poisoned already tense relations between Britain and Argentina. The Match situates the 1986 clash as part of a continuum of strife, dating back at least to the arrival in 1765 of a British sea captain, John Byron, on the Falklands to claim them for Britain. Other key moments: Argentina’s Antonio Rattín getting sent off during the 1966 World Cup, and Maradona being invited on stage by Queen to sing Another One Bites the Dust during their mammoth 1981 South American tour. Continue reading...
